Marine ecosystems encompass some of the most biodiverse and ecologically complex aquatic habitats on Earth. From tropical coral reefs and coastal mangrove forests to the vast pelagic ocean and deep abyssal hydrothermal vents, marine biodiversity sustains planetary biogeochemical cycles. Microscopic phytoplankton inhabiting sunlit epipelagic surface waters perform photosynthesis on a massive scale, producing substantial atmospheric oxygen while forming the primary trophic foundation for pelagic food webs comprising zooplankton, crustaceans, teleost fish, and cetaceans.

Coral reefs, often characterized as underwater rainforests, provide critical benthic shelter, feeding grounds, and nursery zones for thousands of specialized marine species. Scleractinian stony corals maintain mutualistic symbioses with zooxanthellae dinoflagellates, which supply metabolic nutrients through photosynthesis in exchange for inorganic calcification substrates. Ocean currents, thermohaline circulation, and coastal upwelling transport essential dissolved nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicates across ocean basins, regulating global marine nutrient distributions and supporting thriving coastal fisheries.

Anthropogenic stressors, including anthropogenic ocean acidification, marine heatwaves, and coral bleaching, pose severe risks to marine calcifying organisms and fragile coral reef architectures. As oceanic carbon dioxide absorption lowers seawater pH, the saturation state of calcium carbonate decreases, impeding the biomineralization of mollusk shells, echinoderms, and coral skeletons. Marine conservation initiatives, including marine protected areas, artificial reefs, and benthic habitat restoration, are vital for preserving ocean resilience, preventing trophic collapse, and protecting endangered marine fauna.
